newsitem.title: UK: UK rate rise speculation soars as inflation jumps.
newsitem.headline: UK rate rise speculation soars as inflation jumps.

text.p: The odds of an increase in Britain's 6.5 percent official interest rates on Thursday shortened dramatically after stronger-than-expected June inflation data.
Underlying retail prices rose to an annual 2.7 percent, after hitting the official 2.5 percent target briefly in May.

Market speculation raged that the increase in rates this week could be as high as 50 basis points but economists said this was an overreaction and a 25 basis point rise was still more likely because much of the leap in the RPI was down to special factors.

"I don't think the Bank of England are going to do 50 basis points. The sectors which have shown the sharpest rises, like seasonal food, tend to be quite erratic and we could well see it unwound in future months," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr said.
"I'd be particularly surprised given the strength of sterling, it would just make it ratchet up even further," he said.
Sterling moved up through 2.97 marks after the data, to levels not seen since May 1991, as talk of higher rates spiralled.

In the interest rate futures market, prices see-sawed on the news. LIFFE September gilts tumbled as low as 114-15/32 before recovering to 114-22/32, down only 4/32 from Monday's close whilst the September short sterling contract lost four basis points at 92.81.

CIBC chief economist David Coleman said the market had failed initially to pay attention to the detail of the figures. "The market is selling gilts and selling short sterling because it rained in June," he said.

"The market's nervousness about the outcome of this week's Bank of England meeting is understandable but setting interest rates according to the weather might be stretching the bearishness a little too far." The Bank of England begins its two-day Monetary Policy Committee meeting at 1400 GMT on Wednesday, with its decision on interest rates due to be announced at 1100 GMT on Thursday.

Coleman argued that the shock five percent rise in seasonal food prices had distorted the data upwards and suggested that the high level of prices was a result of the wettest weather in June on record. The rise in June was the first for six years and the largest increase since 1978.
"Overall the figures really weren't bad with six out of the 14 categories actually showing price falls," he said.
He said bellwether categories such as clothing and footwear and household goods had actually fallen in June and were likely to drop further in July.

Falls in prices in these sectors are all the more remarkable because of the strength of consumer spending overall. "The clear implication is that consumers remain extremely sensitive to price and continue to demand value for money even when spending their huge windfall gains from de-mutualising building societies," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.
British consumers have received some 30 billion stg in special payments from building societies which are merging or floating on the stock exchange and have been using the money for a spending orgy.
Loynes said that the increases in duty announced at last week's budget would boost the RPI in July but the June increase should be looked upon as a temporary setback, nevertheless.
A rise in petrol prices in June, which has since been reversed, was one of the special factors which boosted June RPI as well as the seasonal food price increases.
"The prices of tomatoes and cauliflower will not be the key determinants of where inflation lies in a year's time," he said.
"That will be decided by cost pressures and consumer attitudes towards price, and on both of those factors these figures bring very encouraging news."
